core: The institutional distinction: jails are locally operated and hold people pretrial and on short sentences; prisons are state or federal and hold sentenced people serving longer terms
Who operates and who pays for each institution, illustrated with primary law (California Penal Code sections 4000 and 4015; 18 U.S.C. 3621 and 4042)
Security levels and classification: the five federal security levels, statutory designation factors, and the PREA intake screening jails must run within 72 hours
Length of stay and population stability: 32-day average jail stay versus multi-year prison terms
The admissions-versus-population distinction, including why BJS jail and prison counts must not be added
Verified, dated BJS population trends for jails (midyear 2023) and prisons (yearend 2023)
Private facilities and their measured share of the prison population
Women in custody in each setting and their different growth pattern
Mental illness and substance use disorders, concentrated more heavily in jails
Conditions-of-confinement law at survey depth: Estelle v. Gamble, Farmer v. Brennan, Bell v. Wolfish, the Prison Litigation Reform Act, and Brown v. Plata
The Prison Rape Elimination Act and the DOJ national standards at 28 C.F.R. Part 115

claims.claim: BJS defines a jail as a confinement facility generally operated under the authority of a sheriff, police chief, or county or city administrator, holding people before and after arraignment (usually beyond 72 hours) and people sentenced to incarceration of one year or less; it defines a prison as a long-term facility run by a state or the federal government that typically holds people sentenced to more than one year, with sentence length varying by state.

Jails are locally operated and locally funded. California Penal Code section 4000 provides that the common jails in the several counties are kept by the sheriffs of those counties, and section 4015 requires the sheriff to receive all persons committed by competent authority and directs the county board of supervisors to provide food, clothing, and bedding, with the expense paid out of the county treasury.

Federal imprisonment is run centrally: 18 U.S.C. 4042(a)(1) puts the Bureau of Prisons in charge of the management and regulation of all federal penal and correctional institutions, and 18 U.S.C. 3621(b) gives the Bureau, not the sentencing court, the power to designate the place of imprisonment, subject to bed availability, the prisoner's security designation, programmatic and health needs, court recommendations, the resources of the facility contemplated, and the nature of the offense.

At midyear 2023 local jails held 664,200 people in custody, 70 percent (467,600) of them unconvicted and 30 percent (196,600) convicted; 75 percent (500,300) were held on felony offenses; the jail incarceration rate was 198 per 100,000 U.S. residents, down from 231 a decade earlier.

At yearend 2023, correctional authorities had jurisdiction over 1,254,224 people in state or federal prisons (1,097,597 state, 156,627 federal), 96 percent of whom (1,210,300) were sentenced to more than one year; the total was 2 percent above 2022 but 20.5 percent below the 2013 figure of 1,576,950, and the imprisonment rate was 360 sentenced prisoners per 100,000 U.S. residents, down 25 percent from 479 in 2013.

Jails churn far faster than prisons. From July 2022 to June 2023 local jails recorded 7.6 million admissions against an average daily population of 664,800, and people admitted spent an average of 32 days in custody before release; in calendar 2023 states and the FBOP recorded 472,300 admissions of sentenced prisoners and 453,200 releases against a sentenced population of 1,210,300.

BJS jail and prison counts must not be added. The midyear 2023 jail custody count (664,200) plus the yearend 2023 prison jurisdiction count (1,254,224) is 1,918,424, whereas BJS's own combined figure for people incarcerated in prisons or local jails at yearend 2023 is 1,852,900 — about 65,000 lower, matching the 65,600 prisoners under state or federal jurisdiction whom BJS reports were held in local jails and who therefore appear in both series.

Incarceration rates differ sharply by race and ethnicity as BJS measures them: at midyear 2023 the jail incarceration rate for Black U.S. residents was 552 per 100,000, 3.6 times the rate for white residents (155 per 100,000), with American Indian and Alaska Native residents second at 425 and Hispanic residents at 143; at yearend 2023, 33 percent of sentenced state or federal prisoners were Black, 31 percent white, and 23 percent Hispanic. These are measurements of who is in custody and BJS does not present them as causal explanations.

The Federal Bureau of Prisons operates 118 institutions at five security levels — minimum, low, medium, high, and administrative — assigned on the basis of features such as external patrols, towers, security barriers, detection devices, housing type, internal security features, and the staff-to-inmate ratio.

Jails must also classify, on a much shorter clock: 28 C.F.R. 115.41 requires an objective screening instrument at intake, ordinarily within 72 hours of arrival, assessing each person's risk of being sexually abused or sexually abusive, with reassessment within 30 days, and 28 C.F.R. 115.42 requires that information to inform housing, bed, work, education, and program assignments.

In 2023, 154,200 people under state or federal jurisdiction — 12 percent of all prisoners — were held in privately operated prison facilities (88,600) or local jails (65,600); the private-prison count fell almost 3 percent from 91,300 in 2022; four states (Montana, New Mexico, Arizona, and Tennessee) held more than a quarter of their people in private facilities; and the FBOP reported holding no prisoners in secure private prisons.

Women are a larger share of jail populations than prison populations and are growing faster in prison: 95,100 women were in jail at midyear 2023 (14 percent of the jail population but 23 percent of admissions, with an average stay of 19 days against 36 for men), while 91,100 women were in prison at yearend 2023 (7 percent of the prison population), up 3.8 percent from 2022 against a 1.8 percent increase for men, with female counts rising in 41 states and male counts in 38.

Indicators of mental health problems and substance use disorders are more prevalent in jails than prisons and far more prevalent than in the general population: in the 2011-12 National Inmate Survey, 26 percent of jail inmates and 14 percent of prisoners met the threshold for serious psychological distress in the prior 30 days against 5 percent of the standardized general population, and 44 percent of jail inmates and 37 percent of prisoners had been told by a mental health professional that they had a mental disorder; in the 2007-2009 National Inmate Surveys, 63 percent of sentenced jail inmates and 58 percent of state prisoners met DSM-IV criteria for drug dependence or abuse against roughly 5 percent of adults generally.

Estelle v. Gamble, 429 U.S. 97 (1976), held that deliberate indifference by prison personnel to a prisoner's serious illness or injury is cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment, but that the respondent's own claim failed because medical staff saw him on 17 occasions in three months and the failure to order an X-ray was at most malpractice cognizable in state court.

Farmer v. Brennan, 511 U.S. 825 (1994), held that a prison official is liable under the Eighth Amendment for deliberate indifference to inmate health or safety only if the official knows that inmates face a substantial risk of serious harm and disregards it by failing to take reasonable measures; deliberate indifference is subjective recklessness, more than negligence and less than purpose, though a factfinder may infer knowledge from the obviousness of a risk, and officials who respond reasonably are not liable even if harm occurs.

Bell v. Wolfish, 441 U.S. 520 (1979), held that conditions of pretrial detention are evaluated under due process by asking whether they amount to punishment; absent an expressed intent to punish, a condition reasonably related to a legitimate nonpunitive governmental objective is not punishment.

The Prison Litigation Reform Act restricts prisoner conditions litigation: 42 U.S.C. 1997e(a) requires exhaustion of available administrative remedies, 1997e(e) bars federal actions for mental or emotional injury without a prior showing of physical injury or the commission of a sexual act, 1997e(d) caps attorney's fees, and 1997e(h) defines 'prisoner' to include people merely accused or detained, so the restrictions apply in jails as well as prisons.

18 U.S.C. 3626(a)(1)(A) requires prospective relief in prison-conditions cases to be narrowly drawn, extend no further than necessary, and be the least intrusive means, with substantial weight given to any adverse impact on public safety, and 3626(a)(3) permits only a three-judge court to enter a prison population cap, after a failed less-intrusive order and on clear and convincing evidence that crowding is the primary cause of the violation and no other relief will remedy it.

BJS reported that after the Prison Litigation Reform Act took effect, civil rights petitions filed by state and federal prisoners in U.S. district courts fell from 41,679 in 1995 to 25,504 in 2000, and the filing rate fell from 37 to 19 per 1,000 prisoners, while habeas corpus petitions rose over the same period; BJS characterized the PLRA as appearing to have caused the decrease.

Brown v. Plata, 563 U.S. 493 (2011), affirmed 5-4 (Kennedy, J.) a three-judge court's order under the PLRA requiring California to reduce its prison population to 137.5 percent of design capacity within two years; at the time of trial California's correctional facilities held some 156,000 people, nearly double design capacity, and the required reduction was estimated as high as 46,000 people.

The Prison Rape Elimination Act of 2003 establishes a zero-tolerance standard for prison rape and directs the Attorney General to adopt national standards; the standards are codified at 28 C.F.R. Part 115 in separate subparts for adult prisons and jails, lockups, community confinement facilities, and juvenile facilities, require each facility to be audited at least once every three years by a DOJ-certified auditor external to the agency with the agency bearing the burden of demonstrating compliance, and 34 U.S.C. 30307(e) reduces by 5 percent a state's covered DOJ grant funds for prison purposes unless its chief executive certifies full compliance or provides a qualifying assurance.

Jail capacity is not the binding constraint nationally even though individual jails are crowded: at midyear 2023 there were 915,800 jail beds and 73 percent were occupied, down from an 84 percent occupancy rate in 2013, while 12 percent of jail jurisdictions were operating above their rated capacity.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many people are incarcerated in the United States on a given day
positions: Adding BJS's headline jail count (664,200 at midyear 2023) to its headline prison count (1,254,224 at yearend 2023) yields 1,918,424.
BJS's own combined figure for people incarcerated in prisons or local jails at yearend 2023 is 1,852,900.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The published totals are not additive. Prisoners under state or federal jurisdiction who are physically held in local jails (65,600 in 2023) are counted in both series; the reference dates differ (midyear versus yearend); and the jail series excludes the six states with integrated systems whose populations are counted as prisoners. The lesson uses BJS's own combined figure and teaches the arithmetic of the gap rather than summing categories.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How current the mental health and substance use estimates for jail populations are
positions: The BJS estimates most often quoted come from the 2011-12 and 2007-2009 National Inmate Surveys.
More recent BJS surveys of prison populations exist, but no comparable recent national estimate for the jail population was located.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson dates each estimate explicitly, states that they describe the populations surveyed at that time, and does not present them as current-year measurements.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the PLRA caused the drop in prisoner civil rights filings
positions: BJS reported a large drop in civil rights petitions and filing rates after 1995 and stated the PLRA appears to have resulted in the decrease.
The decline is observational; the PLRA was enacted alongside AEDPA and other changes.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the measured before-and-after figures, attributes the causal characterization to BJS rather than asserting it independently, and notes that habeas filings rose over the same period.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about jails or prisons at all — its In 30 Seconds, College Version, vocabulary, worked example, and question bank were subject-agnostic placeholder text ('a foundational concept', 'a label on a toolbox drawer') that named no institution, statistic, statute, or case.
The draft's vocabulary list defined 'context', 'evidence', and 'application' rather than any corrections term.
The draft asserted that the topic is 'a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions' without identifying what it builds toward.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire lesson with researched content built on BJS primary publications, Supreme Court opinions read in the U.S. Reports, the U.S. Code, and the Code of Federal Regulations.
Added the operating-authority and funding distinction with primary statutory support rather than a general assertion that jails are 'local'.

Added the admissions-versus-population distinction as the worked example, including the arithmetic that reproduces BJS's published 32-day average stay and the arithmetic that exposes the double-counting trap.
Dated every statistic to its BJS reference period (midyear 2023 for jails, yearend 2023 for prisons, 2011-12 and 2007-2009 for the inmate surveys).
Added an explicit statement that the lesson is educational material and not legal advice, and that state law varies.
rightsIssues: Supreme Court opinions, the U.S. Code, the Code of Federal Regulations, and California codified statutes are U.S. government or state edicts and are treated as public domain; short quoted phrases from opinions and statutes are used for accuracy and attributed inline.

BJS publications and the Bureau of Prisons website are federal government works used as REFERENCE_ONLY: all figures were extracted and restated in original prose, and no BJS wording was reproduced beyond short definitional phrases attributed to BJS.
No source's prose structure was followed; the lesson is an original synthesis.

sourceRecords.title: Estelle v. Gamble, 429 U.S. 97 (1976)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (via govinfo, U.S. Reports)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound-volume opinion PDF from govinfo. Supports the holding that deliberate indifference by prison personnel to a prisoner's serious illness or injury is cruel and unusual punishment; the Eighth Amendment framing through evolving standards of decency and the unnecessary and wanton infliction of pain; the government's obligation to provide medical care to those it incarcerates; and the outcome for Gamble himself, who was seen 17 times in three months so that the failure to order an X-ray was at most malpractice cognizable in state court. Marshall, J., delivered the opinion.

sourceRecords.title: Farmer v. Brennan, 511 U.S. 825 (1994)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (via govinfo, U.S. Reports)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound-volume opinion PDF from govinfo. Supports the duty to provide humane conditions of confinement (adequate food, clothing, shelter, and medical care, and protection from violence at the hands of other prisoners); the two-part objective-plus-subjective test; the definition of deliberate indifference as subjective recklessness, more than negligence and less than purpose; that a factfinder may infer knowledge from the obviousness of a risk; and that officials who respond reasonably to a known risk are not liable even if harm is not averted. Souter, J., delivered the opinion of the Court.

sourceRecords.title: Bell v. Wolfish, 441 U.S. 520 (1979)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (via govinfo, U.S. Reports)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound-volume opinion PDF from govinfo. Supports the point that conditions claims by people not yet convicted are analyzed under due process rather than the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause, and that the inquiry is whether a condition amounts to punishment: absent an expressed intent to punish, a condition reasonably related to a legitimate nonpunitive governmental objective does not amount to punishment. The case arose from a federally operated short-term detention facility, which is why it matters for the jail side of this lesson. Rehnquist, J., delivered the opinion.

sourceRecords.title: Brown v. Plata, 563 U.S. 493 (2011)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (via govinfo, U.S. Reports)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound-volume opinion PDF from govinfo. Supports the consolidation of Coleman (mental health care, filed 1990) and Plata (medical care, filed 2001); the convening of a three-judge court under the PLRA; the order to reduce California's prison population to 137.5% of design capacity within two years; the figure of some 156,000 people held at the time of trial, nearly double design capacity; the estimated required reduction of as much as 46,000 people; and the lineup - Kennedy, J., for the Court joined by Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan, with Scalia, J., dissenting joined by Thomas, and Alito, J., dissenting joined by Roberts, C.J.

sourceRecords.title: 42 U.S.C. 1997e - Suits by prisoners
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives
sourceRecords.notes: Read the current text (laws in effect on August 18, 2026). Supports the Prison Litigation Reform Act's core restrictions: subsection (a) exhaustion of available administrative remedies before any action about prison conditions; subsection (c) mandatory dismissal of frivolous or malicious actions and those failing to state a claim; subsection (d) attorney's fee limits including the 150% cap on the hourly rate and the up-to-25% offset from a monetary judgment; subsection (e) the physical-injury or sexual-act prerequisite for mental or emotional injury claims; and subsection (h), which defines 'prisoner' to include a person merely accused or detained, so the statute reaches jails as well as prisons.
